name: Fenra Hibiscus-Ginger Stim Rocks
manufacturer: Fenra Street Foods (unlicensed street brand, Shelf / Tier 1)
description: Popping candy rocks in hibiscus-ginger flavor with an unlicensed low-grade stimulant compound mixed into the sugar base. Sold in small foil envelopes with hand-stamped branding, distributed through informal Shelf networks. The pop-and-crackle texture is a feature and a delivery mechanism.
flavor_profile: Tart hibiscus and sharp fresh ginger with a faint chemical sweetness from the stim base; the popping sensation intensifies the ginger heat briefly
cultural_context: Fenra rocks are technically illegal due to unlicensed stimulant content, but enforcement on the Shelf is inconsistent. They're popular with teenagers, night-shift workers who can't afford licensed stim-candy, and anyone who finds the popping texture entertaining. The hand-stamped branding changes design every few weeks — partly aesthetic, partly to complicate enforcement identification. Regulars collect the different stamp variations.
story_hooks: The stimulant compound in a recent Fenra batch is significantly stronger than usual — someone upstream in the supply chain made a substitution, and the Shelf is about to feel it.
A Corponation enforcement officer has been looking the other way on Fenra for six months; the question is whether it's corruption, sympathy, or something more strategic.

A Tier 3 researcher studying unlicensed bioactive compounds in Shelf food products has been documenting Fenra's formula changes over time and has noticed a pattern that suggests the 'unlicensed' manufacturer has real chemistry training.
